summary: Teaches 9–11 year olds the palaeontology workflow as a PROCEDURE run in order — prospect, excavate with the right tool, record context before lifting, plaster-jacket, transport, prepare in the lab, then study, compare and publish. The core insight is that method and tool choice protect irreplaceable evidence: where and how a fossil lay is data lost forever if not recorded before removal, and the right care turns 'an old bone' into scientific evidence. Learners perform the sequence and experience the cost of wrong tools or skipped steps.
misconceptions: 'You just dig fossils out fast' — excavation is slow, careful, and documented; speed destroys evidence.
'Where a fossil was found doesn't matter, only the bone' — context (layer, position, associates) is crucial data.
'Any tool will do' — the wrong tool damages delicate specimens.
'The work ends when the fossil is out of the ground' — preparation, comparison and publication are essential later stages.
'One person makes the discovery alone' — palaeontology is collaborative and peer-reviewed.

activities.title: Lead palaeontologist: run the dig in order
steps: Prospect a landscape and choose where to dig — crumbling sedimentary badlands where bones of the right age surface, not granite hills — and say why.
Pick a tool from a tray at a find: try a heavy pick/hammer and observe the fragile bone cracking, then switch to a fine brush and awl and watch the fossil emerge intact.
Before lifting the bone, complete a required recording step — photograph, grid-map and label the bone's position and rock layer in place — and only then proceed to removal.

Once the bone is recorded and exposed on a pedestal of rock, plaster-jacket it in place, then undercut and lift the jacketed block for transport. Next, prepare it in the lab (note that rushing the cleaning strips away fine detail).
Compare the prepared fossil to known skeletons, write a scientific description of it, and submit that description for peer review and publication.
State in one sentence why the same bone can become valuable scientific evidence (and perhaps a museum display) if the method is followed, but just a curio if it isn't.
activities.insight: Each step exists for a reason: recording position captures data that vanishes once a fossil is lifted, the right tool protects a fragile specimen, and lab preparation, comparison and publication are what make a find into scientific evidence rather than just an old bone.

activities.title: Explore an annotated dig-site scene
steps: Move through zones of a labelled scene — field dig → plaster jacket → lab prep bench → study/comparison → publication — and reveal at each what happens and which tool is used.
At the field zone, identify which tools are fine (brush, awl) and which are coarse (hammer, pick), and which belong on delicate bone.
At the lab zone, look at a fossil being cleaned of surrounding rock (matrix) under magnification and describe why this stage matters.
activities.insight: Intended to build the vocabulary and mental map of the full workflow and the tools and purpose of each stage, from field to lab to publication.

activities.title: Check: order and justify the workflow
steps: Put the workflow stages in order: prospect for exposed fossils → carefully expose the bone with small tools and record its position and rock layer (photograph, grid-map, label) → wrap it in a plaster jacket while it still sits on a pedestal of rock → undercut and lift the jacketed block → transport to the lab → prepare and clean in the lab → study and publish.
Match each tool to its task, and explain why a plaster jacket is used (to hold the fragile fossil and its surrounding rock together while it is lifted out and transported).
Answer why recording exactly where and in which rock layer a fossil was found matters before removal.
Explain what could be lost forever if a fossil is dug out carelessly.
activities.insight: Confirms the learner can both sequence the process — including recording context before removal — and justify the care steps, reasoning about what rushing would destroy.

activities.title: Interview a working palaeontologist
steps: Prepare and ask questions of a field palaeontologist, including: 'What would you never do at a dig site, and why?' and 'Why do you record where a bone was found before lifting it?'
After the discussion, summarise one thing that changed or confirmed your understanding of the workflow.
activities.insight: Shows palaeontology as collaborative, methodical work — with real roles such as prospector, preparator and curator — rather than lone treasure-hunting.

activities.title: Optional: uncover a bone in a 3D quarry
steps: At a 3D quarry, choose depth and tool to brush away surrounding rock and reveal a partly buried bone, exposing how it lies in space.
Describe the spatial arrangement of the bone before removing it, and record its position.
activities.insight: Adds a sense of embodiment to excavation and makes the spatial arrangement of a buried specimen concrete.

checkQuestion: A palaeontologist has just spotted a dinosaur bone poking out of a hillside. Put these jobs in the order she'd actually do them, and as you go explain WHY each step is done: study and publish; wrap it in a plaster jacket; dig it out carefully with small tools; transport it to the lab; prepare and clean it in the lab; prospect for exposed fossils. If any step would be risky to rush, say what would go wrong.
checkAnswer: Prospect for exposed fossils → dig it out carefully with small tools → wrap it in a plaster jacket → transport it to the lab → prepare and clean it in the lab → study and publish. Careful small-tool excavation avoids breaking the fragile fossil and preserves its context; the plaster jacket protects the freed fossil during transport.
